title: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump
description_short: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump
description_medium: During a May 2020 Fox News appearance, Eric Trump claimed that COVID-19 would “magically” disappear after the election and said stay-at-home orders were meant to deprive his father of campaign rallies. He also repeated a baseless claim about White House reporters wearing masks only for cameras. The comments treated public-health restrictions as political sabotage, not infection control.
description_long:
On May 16, 2020, Eric Trump appeared on Fox News with Jeanine Pirro and said the pandemic was a “hoax” being used to hurt his father politically. He argued that stay-at-home orders deprived Donald Trump of large campaign rallies and predicted that coronavirus would disappear after the November election. Eric also claimed that White House reporters wore masks only while cameras were on.

The remarks came as the United States was responding to rising COVID-19 infections and deaths. They recast public-health restrictions as an effort to damage Trump rather than as measures intended to limit transmission. Eric’s statements were political claims, not evidence about why state officials issued orders or when the virus would end. Pirro did not challenge his claims during the segment and added her own assertion that Democrats wanted to frighten people away from voting in person. The episode shows how the Trump campaign’s family surrogates used pandemic restrictions as an election argument.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Eric Trump: COVID is a hoax, state lockdowns are a weapon against Trump

title: Trump: Anthony Scaramucci warns that Trump is a threat to the nation, endorses Biden
description_short: Trump: Anthony Scaramucci warns that Trump is a threat to the nation, endorses Biden
description_medium: On August 24, 2020, former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci warned that Trump endangered the country and endorsed Joe Biden. In a public statement before the Republican National Convention, he cited Trump’s attacks on institutions, allies and the press, and his handling of the pandemic. Scaramucci had served in the White House for less than two weeks in 2017.
description_long:
On August 24, 2020, Anthony Scaramucci publicly endorsed Joe Biden and warned that Trump was a danger to the country and the Constitution. Scaramucci had served as White House communications director for less than two weeks in 2017. Before the Republican National Convention, he apologized for having supported Trump and urged Republicans to choose a different direction.

In his statement, Scaramucci accused Trump of undermining the criminal-justice system, damaging democratic institutions, alienating allies and bullying the press. He also criticized Trump’s treatment of science during the COVID-19 pandemic and the use of force against peaceful protesters. Scaramucci argued that Biden was closer to the decency and institutional restraint he wanted the Republican Party to represent. These were the reasons Scaramucci gave for breaking with Trump and backing Biden; the statement documents a former administration official’s political judgment, not a formal finding about Trump’s conduct. His short tenure made the endorsement notable, but the public act was his 2020 break with the president.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Anthony Scaramucci warns that Trump is a threat to the nation, endorses Biden

title: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
description_short: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
description_medium: Acting Homeland Security Secretary Chad Wolf told senators in September 2020 that Russia was actively interfering in the election and seeking to denigrate Joe Biden. He said the United States faced interference threats from Russia, China and Iran, but that current intelligence did not show China or Iran had carried out attacks. The distinction was between active Russian operations and broader foreign threats.
description_long:
On September 23, 2020, Acting Homeland Security Secretary Chad Wolf told senators that Russia was actively engaged in election interference and sought to denigrate Democratic nominee Joe Biden. He also said the United States faced election-related threats from China and Iran, while noting that intelligence at the time did not show those countries had carried out attacks.

The testimony distinguished between Russian activity and the other countries’ potential interests or threats. The linked account emphasized “Russia, and only Russia” to challenge political claims that China and Iran were also carrying out active interference. A separate Reuters report described a whistleblower complaint alleging that Wolf had told a former aide to stop preparing assessments of Russian interference and to reduce the emphasis on white-supremacist activity. That allegation concerned the handling of intelligence assessments; it does not change what Wolf said in his September testimony. The record is a statement before Congress about the threat picture as officials described it in 2020.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election

title: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19
description_short: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19
description_medium: White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows tested positive for COVID-19 around the November 3, 2020, election, the linked account reported. Advisers said he began telling staff after early election results came in, but the date he learned of the infection was unclear. Six other people were also reported positive, including campaign aide Nick Trainer and White House and campaign staff.
description_long:
Mark Meadows, then White House chief of staff, tested positive for COVID-19 around November 3, 2020, the linked account reported. Advisers said he began notifying people in his circle after early election results came in. The news became public late that Friday. At the time, it was not clear when Meadows had learned he was infected or whether he had symptoms.

The account also named Trump campaign aide Nick Trainer and said the White House later confirmed positive tests for at least four other officials and one campaign staffer. Representative Matt Gaetz was reported to have told associates he tested positive, but he said he had tested positive for antibodies and did not have COVID-19. The report placed Meadows’s infection amid a wider cluster of cases among people connected to the White House and campaign. Its timeline left open when Meadows may have been infectious and what exposure occurred before staff were notified; the reported positive tests alone do not identify where transmission took place.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19

title: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director
description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director
description_medium: On November 5, 2020, Steve Bannon said on his “War Room” podcast that he wanted Anthony Fauci and FBI Director Christopher Wray fired and their heads displayed on pikes outside the White House. Bannon’s spokesperson said he meant the Tudor-era reference metaphorically. Twitter permanently suspended the podcast account, and YouTube removed the episode for violating its policy against glorifying or inciting violence.
description_long:
Former Trump adviser Steve Bannon made the remarks on his “War Room: Pandemic” podcast while discussing a hypothetical second Trump term. He said it should begin by firing Anthony Fauci and FBI Director Christopher Wray, then invoked Tudor-era executions and said he would put their heads on pikes outside the White House as a warning to federal officials.

Bannon’s spokeswoman said he was speaking metaphorically and had not called for actual violence. Twitter permanently suspended the podcast account, citing its policy against glorifying violence, and YouTube removed the episode for violating its policy against inciting violence. Bannon made the comments while free on bond in a federal case accusing him of defrauding donors to a border-wall nonprofit; prosecutors did not announce a response to the remarks in the report. The episode documents violent rhetoric and platform enforcement, not a government order or an attack on Fauci or Wray. Bannon’s statement and his representative’s explanation should both remain part of the account.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director

title: Trump: Steve Bannon caught using Facebook to push election lies to 2.45 million followers
description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon caught using Facebook to push election lies to 2.45 million followers
description_medium: Facebook removed seven pages that it linked to Steve Bannon and that together had more than 2.45 million followers, citing misinformation about voter fraud and the election. The Washington Post reported that the network promoted “Stop the Steal” claims. Facebook also restricted Bannon’s personal page from posting, but did not remove that page.
description_long:
Facebook removed seven pages with a combined following of more than 2.45 million that it linked to Steve Bannon, the Washington Post reported in November 2020. The pages promoted claims about voter fraud and the legitimacy of the election results, including messages associated with the “Stop the Steal” effort. Facebook said the network used inauthentic behavior tactics.

The company also restricted Bannon’s personal Facebook page from posting content, but left the page online. The distinction matters: the platform removed the network of pages and limited his own account, rather than deleting his personal profile. The report connected Bannon’s online activity to attempts to undermine trust in the vote count, but it did not provide the reach of individual posts or name every page in the network. The action records Facebook’s enforcement decision and its stated reason; it does not establish how many users saw or believed the claims.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Steve Bannon caught using Facebook to push election lies to 2.45 million followers
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon caught using Facebook to push election lies to 2.45 million followers

title: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
description_short: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
description_medium: Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander said on a livestream that he and Representatives Paul Gosar, Mo Brooks and Andy Biggs devised a plan to pressure Congress on January 6, 2021. He described it as a “loud war” outside the Capitol while lawmakers counted electoral votes. The linked account reports Alexander’s claim; it does not independently establish the lawmakers’ agreement or role.
description_long:
In a December 28, 2020, livestream, Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander said he had come up with the January 6 plan with Representatives Paul Gosar, Mo Brooks and Andy Biggs. Alexander said the four had schemed to put “maximum pressure” on Congress while members counted electoral votes, so that protesters outside could sway Republican lawmakers. He called the planned demonstration a “loud war.”

The statement tied Alexander’s post-election mobilization to named members of Congress, but it was Alexander’s account of their involvement. The linked article says the lawmakers denied knowing him, while describing prior public events and statements that Alexander cited as evidence of connections. The claim therefore documents what Alexander said before January 6; it does not by itself prove that each lawmaker agreed to a joint plan or knew how events would unfold. His remarks concerned a planned protest and pressure campaign at the Capitol, not an explicit prediction of the later assault.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol

title: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
description_short: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
description_medium: Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller ordered the NSA to install Michael Ellis as its top lawyer in January 2021. Ellis began the job on January 19 and was placed on leave the next day, when the Defense Department inspector general opened an investigation into the appointment. The move came days before Trump left office and followed months in which Ellis had been named but not installed.
description_long:
On January 16, 2021, Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller ordered the director of the National Security Agency to install Michael Ellis as the agency’s general counsel. Ellis had been named for the role in November but had not yet taken office. The NSA installed him on January 19, his first day in the position.

On January 20, Ellis was placed on leave as the Defense Department inspector general opened an investigation into his appointment. The timing put the installation in the final days of Trump’s term. Ellis had previously worked for Representative Devin Nunes and served in intelligence roles at the National Security Council. The linked reporting does not establish that his selection or prior work caused the inspector general’s inquiry, but it records the directive, rapid installation and immediate leave. The sequence raised questions about the appointment process and the agency’s handling of it, while the investigation was still underway.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer

title: Trump: Don Jr. gives deposition surrounding the misuse of funds by Trump's inaugural committee
description_short: Trump: Don Jr. gives deposition surrounding the misuse of funds by Trump's inaugural committee
description_medium: Donald Trump Jr. was deposed on February 11, 2021, in the District of Columbia’s lawsuit over inaugural committee spending. The questioning covered a nearly $50,000 hotel-room block contracted by the Trump Organization and paid by the committee. D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine said witnesses gave conflicting accounts of the charges and sought more time for discovery.
description_long:
District of Columbia Attorney General Karl Racine deposed Donald Trump Jr. on February 11, 2021, as part of a lawsuit over the 2017 presidential inaugural committee’s spending. The questioning focused on nearly $50,000 the committee paid for rooms at the Loews Madison Hotel under a contract signed by the Trump Organization. Trump Jr.’s executive assistant handled the contract, which was signed by his friend Gentry Beach.

The District’s lawsuit alleged that the committee misused donations to benefit Trump family businesses, including by spending more than $1 million at the Trump International Hotel. Racine told the court that witnesses gave conflicting explanations for the room charges and said Trump Jr. could not say whether the people associated with the rooms had donated to the committee. The deposition was evidence gathering in a civil case, not a ruling that the allegations were true. Racine sought additional time to collect records and question more witnesses, leaving the dispute unresolved at the time of the report.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Don Jr. gives deposition surrounding the misuse of funds by Trump's inaugural committee
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Don Jr. gives deposition surrounding the misuse of funds by Trump's inaugural committee

title: Trump: The FBI publishes ‘Wanted' posters for Russians involved in 2016 election and more
description_short: Trump: The FBI publishes ‘Wanted' posters for Russians involved in 2016 election and more
description_medium: The FBI circulated wanted posters seeking Russian nationals linked to its 2016 election-interference investigation. The supplied account names Konstantin Kilimnik and says the FBI sought him on obstruction and conspiracy charges. The poster date, full list of subjects, exact allegations and later case status are not available from the linked page.
description_long: The FBI circulated wanted posters seeking Russian nationals linked to its 2016 election-interference investigation. The record names Konstantin Viktorovich Kilimnik and says the FBI sought him on obstruction and conspiracy charges in Washington, D.C., and elsewhere. It does not establish the poster’s exact date, the full list of subjects, the underlying charge wording or the later status of each case. Those details require the poster and charging documents.
